name: Bandeau Brassiere
summary: The first modern brassiere: a light, unboned band or two cups of silk, cotton and lace, tied at the back. It replaced the corset above the waist and then flattened the bust for the 1920s dress.

philosophy.core_thesis: The body needs a light band, not a cage: a soft brassiere carries the bust and leaves the waist free for the new, loose dress.
design_principles: Make the brassiere of two small panels joined at the centre front by a short strip.
Leave out all bone and steel; hold the shape with the cut and with a tape.
Tie or hook the band at the back, and set it low enough to leave the back bare.
Cut the band 12 to 20 cm deep, so that it covers the bust and no more.
Make the body in fine cotton, silk or crêpe de Chine, and trim the edge with lace.
Fasten the straps with narrow ribbon, tied at the shoulder.
From 1920, cut the band flat to press the bust level with the chest.
anti_patterns: A long boned corset with a busk
Cups of nylon or elastic stretch cloth
A wired, padded cup of the later twentieth century

silhouette.shape: A short, flat band across the chest, with narrow straps, over a plain, straight torso.
silhouette.line: A level line across the chest; there is no waist and no bust point.
silhouette.fit: Light and close at the chest; the tape at the back is adjustable.
silhouette.proportion: Band 12 to 20 cm deep; straps 1 to 2 cm wide; centre front 4 to 8 cm.
rules: Cut two panels, and join them at the centre front with a short seam.
Add an elastic or a plain tape at the back and tie it at the side.
Edge the top and the bottom with a narrow lace or a bias strip.
Keep the back low, to fit the dress with a bare back.
Wear it with a chemise or a loose slip, and no corset.

fabrics.rule: Use light, soft cloth of cotton and silk, trim it with lace, and keep it free of bone and steel.

methods: two panels cut from a rectangle
ribbon straps tied at the shoulder
construction.closures: A tie or a hook at the back, and ribbon straps; later versions use a small metal hook and eye.
construction.details: A narrow lace at the top edge, a small ribbon rose at the centre, and elastic at the back in the late 1920s.

surface.pattern: Plain white, ivory or blush; for evening, lace or small embroidery along the edge.
surface.gloss: Cotton and crêpe de Chine at 3–10 GU; satin at 30–55 GU.
surface.wear: A washed brassiere softens and loses its colour; the tape at the back stretches first.

palette.strategy: White, ivory and blush pink, with a few pale tints; the garment stays under the dress and shows no colour.

processes: paper pattern cut in few sizes
bias strips cut and sewn at the edge
tape and ribbon fitted at the back
making.scale: Made at home from two handkerchiefs and a ribbon. Sold in shops from the 1910s. Made in a factory in standard cup sizes from the 1920s.
making.signs: A short band with no bone, a seam at the centre front, a tape at the back, and a narrow lace at the edge.

pieces.form: Backless brassiere of two handkerchiefs joined with ribbon
Flat bandeau of crêpe de Chine with a lace edge
Evening brassiere of satin with a lace top
Step-in chemise of crêpe de Chine
Knitted silk stockings rolled at the knee

emotion.target_response: A sense of ease and freedom: a light body, a flat line and no cage under the dress.

use_cases: a museum label or object study
avoid_when: the brief wants a pointed, wired 1950s bra
the brief wants a boned corset

modifiers.how: Add a long busk, spring-steel bones and a laced back; keep the low bust line.
Flatten the bust with the band, and drop the waist to the hip line.

ornament_level.note: Day bandeaux are plain; evening ones carry lace.
